claim: Eukaryotes have two types of spliceosomes, comprised of either major (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) or minor (U11, U12, U4atac, U6atac; <1%) snRNPs.
source: Eukaryotes have two types of spliceosomes, comprised of either major (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) or minor (U11, U12, U4atac, U6atac; <1%) snRNPs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about spliceosome composition in eukaryotes.

claim: Minor introns are highly conserved despite their poor splicing.
source: The high conservation of minor introns, typically one amidst many major introns in several hundred genes, despite their poor splicing, has been a long-standing enigma.
evidence: This statement references established observations in the field that have been previously documented.

claim: U6atac snRNA has a half-life of less than 2 hours.
source: Here, we discovered that the low abundance minor spliceosome's catalytic snRNP, U6atac, is strikingly unstable (t½<2 hr).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: U6atac level depends on both RNA polymerases II and III.
source: We show that U6atac level depends on both RNA polymerases II and III and can be rapidly increased by cell stress-activated kinase p38MAPK, which stabilizes it, enhancing mRNA expression of hundreds of minor intron-containing genes that are otherwise suppressed by limiting U6atac.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing U6atac decrease after Pol II inhibition (Figure 1A) and discussion of Pol III co-dependence on Pol II.

claim: p38MAPK can rapidly increase U6atac level by stabilizing it.
source: We show that U6atac level depends on both RNA polymerases II and III and can be rapidly increased by cell stress-activated kinase p38MAPK, which stabilizes it, enhancing mRNA expression of hundreds of minor intron-containing genes that are otherwise suppressed by limiting U6atac.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing U6atac increase after anisomycin treatment and stabilization experiments.

claim: Hundreds of minor intron-containing genes are suppressed by limiting U6atac under normal conditions.
source: We show that U6atac level depends on both RNA polymerases II and III and can be rapidly increased by cell stress-activated kinase p38MAPK, which stabilizes it, enhancing mRNA expression of hundreds of minor intron-containing genes that are otherwise suppressed by limiting U6atac.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing that 206 out of 429 expressed minor intron-containing genes were severely down-regulated.

claim: p38MAPK-dependent U6atac modulation can control PTEN expression.
source: Furthermore, p38MAPK-dependent U6atac modulation can control minor intron-containing tumor suppressor PTEN expression and cytokine production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6A showing PTEN splicing changes with anisomycin treatment and U6atac AMO.

claim: p38MAPK-dependent U6atac modulation can control cytokine production.
source: Furthermore, p38MAPK-dependent U6atac modulation can control minor intron-containing tumor suppressor PTEN expression and cytokine production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B,C showing TNF-α and IL-8 changes with U6atac AMO treatment.

claim: Minor introns are embedded molecular switches regulated by U6atac abundance.
source: We propose that minor introns are embedded molecular switches regulated by U6atac abundance, providing a novel post-transcriptional gene expression mechanism and a rationale for the minor spliceosome's evolutionary conservation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vast majority of introns (>200,000) in complex eukaryotes are spliced by the major spliceosome.
source: The vast majority of introns (>200,000) in complex eukaryotes are spliced by the major spliceosome (Wahl et al., 2009), consisting of U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6 snRNPs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wahl et al., 2009.

claim: Approximately 700 minor introns are spliced by the minor spliceosome.
source: However, ∼700 minor introns, also known as U12 introns, are spliced by the much less abundant (<1%) minor spliceosome, consisting of U11, U12, U4atac, U5 and U6atac snRNPs (Hall and Padgett, 1996; Tarn and Steitz, 1996; Patel and Steitz, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall and Padgett, 1996; Tarn and Steitz, 1996; Patel and Steitz, 2003.

claim: Minor introns are found in genes essential for diverse cellular processes.
source: Despite their low occurrence, minor introns, typically one amidst many major introns, are found in genes essential for diverse cellular processes (Burge et al., 1998; Sheth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burge et al., 1998; Sheth et al., 2006.

claim: Minor intron splice site sequences, position and the genes in which they reside are all highly conserved.
source: Their splice site sequences, position and the genes in which they reside are all highly conserved (Basu et al., 2008; Turunen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basu et al., 2008; Turunen et al., 2012.

claim: Previous data suggested that minor introns are generally poorly spliced.
source: However, previous data suggested that minor introns are generally poorly spliced, and therefore the purpose of the minor splicing pathway has been a long-standing mystery, as it has been difficult to rationalize their remarkable conservation and function in splicing alone.
evidence: This references previous observations in the field.

claim: Mutations in U4atac cause microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type I (MOPD I) or Taybi-Linder syndrome (TALS).
source: The importance of the minor spliceosome has been recently underscored by reports that mutations in U4atac cause microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type I (MOPD I) or Taybi-Linder syndrome (TALS) (Abdel-Salam et al., 2011; Edery et al., 2011; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abdel-Salam et al., 2011; Edery et al., 2011; He et al., 2011.

claim: Perturbations in the repertoire of both major and minor snRNPs cause widespread transcriptome and splicing defects in spinal muscular atrophy.
source: We have previously shown that perturbations in the repertoire of both major and minor snRNPs cause widespread transcriptome and splicing defects in spinal muscular atrophy (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Pol II transcription inhibition by Actinomycin D led to a rapid and strong decrease in U6atac, U6 snRNAs, and vault RNAs.
source: Interestingly, Pol II transcription inhibition by Actinomycin D (ActD), as well as by the structurally and chemically unrelated Pol II inhibitor 5,6-Dichloro-1-β-D-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB), led to a rapid and strong decrease in the levels of three ncRNAs transcribed by Pol III: U6atac and U6 snRNAs, and vault RNAs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DRB led to a rapid and strong decrease in U6atac, U6 snRNAs, and vault RNAs.
source: Interestingly, Pol II transcription inhibition by Actinomycin D (ActD), as well as by the structurally and chemically unrelated Pol II inhibitor 5,6-Dichloro-1-β-D-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB), led to a rapid and strong decrease in the levels of three ncRNAs transcribed by Pol III: U6atac and U6 snRNAs, and vault RNAs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pol III transcription shows co-dependence on Pol II, which binds upstream of Pol III at the promoter of these ncRNAs.
source: Previous studies have shown co-dependence of Pol III transcription on Pol II, which binds upstream of Pol III at the promoter of these ncRNAs (Listerman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Listerman et al., 2007.

claim: The decrease in vault RNAs after ActD treatment has been previously observed in mouse cells.
source: The decrease in vault RNAs after ActD treatment has been previously observed in mouse cells (Kickhoefer et al., 2001), and U6 was noted to have a shorter half-life compared to other major snRNAs (Fury and Zieve, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kickhoefer et al., 2001.

claim: U6 has a shorter half-life compared to other major snRNAs.
source: The decrease in vault RNAs after ActD treatment has been previously observed in mouse cells (Kickhoefer et al., 2001), and U6 was noted to have a shorter half-life compared to other major snRNAs (Fury and Zieve, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fury and Zieve, 1996.

claim: This is the first report of U6atac's fast turnover.
source: However, this is the first report of U6atac's fast turnover.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Real-time qPCR validated the short half-life of U6 and U6atac, but not U5.
source: Real-time qPCR validated the short half-life of U6 and U6atac, but not U5, for which the microarray did not predict a change (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HeLa cells arrested in mitosis using nocodazole showed a moderate U6atac decrease.
source: In comparison, HeLa cells arrested in mitosis using nocodazole, which causes transcription by all three types of polymerases to cease, showed a moderate U6atac decrease, whereas translation inhibition with cycloheximide (CHX) caused no significant changes in the levels of the ncRNAs tested (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Translation inhibition with cycloheximide caused no significant changes in the levels of the ncRNAs tested.
source: In comparison, HeLa cells arrested in mitosis using nocodazole, which causes transcription by all three types of polymerases to cease, showed a moderate U6atac decrease, whereas translation inhibition with cycloheximide (CHX) caused no significant changes in the levels of the ncRNAs tested (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In cells, U6atac mostly exists as part of U4atac/U6atac di-snRNP or U4atac/U6atac/U5 tri-snRNP complexes.
source: In cells, U6atac mostly exists as part of U4atac/U6atac di-snRNP or U4atac/U6atac/U5 tri-snRNP complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about U6atac snRNP complexes.

claim: ActD decreased U4atac level by approximately 20% in total RNA.
source: This showed that ActD decreased U4atac level by ∼20% in total RNA, whereas the U4atac/U6atac di-snRNP formation was reduced by >80% (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ActD reduced U4atac/U6atac di-snRNP formation by more than 80%.
source: This showed that ActD decreased U4atac level by ∼20% in total RNA, whereas the U4atac/U6atac di-snRNP formation was reduced by >80% (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: U6atac instability is rate limiting for U4atac/U6atac di-snRNP formation.
source: These results demonstrate the fast turnover and vulnerability of U6atac to transcriptional inhibition, which makes it rate limiting for di-snRNP formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing disproportionate reduction in di-snRNP formation compared to U4atac levels.

claim: An antisense morpholino oligonucleotide (AMO) targeting the 5′ end of U6atac snRNA can rapidly inhibit its activity in cells.
source: To determine the effects of U6atac inactivation on the transcriptome, we used an antisense morpholino oligonucleotide (AMO) that targets the 5′ end of U6atac snRNA to rapidly inhibit its activity in cells (Konig et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Konig et al., 2007 and experimental validation in Figure 2A.

claim: RNase H protection confirmed the binding of the AMO to U6atac snRNP and its efficient interference following an 8 hr transfection with 15 nmole of U6atac AMO.
source: RNase H protection using an antisense DNA probe complementary to the same sequence confirmed the binding of the AMO to U6atac snRNP and its efficient interference following an 8 hr transfection with 15 nmole of U6atac AMO (Figure 2A), which was used for all subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: U6atac AMO, but not control AMO or U6 AMO, resulted in inhibition of minor intron splicing.
source: The specificity and efficiency of the AMOs were verified by RT-PCR showing that U6atac AMO, but not control AMO or U6 AMO, resulted in inhibition of minor intron splicing (Figure 2B), whereas U6 AMO inhibited splicing of only the major introns (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: U6 AMO inhibited splicing of only the major introns.
source: The specificity and efficiency of the AMOs were verified by RT-PCR showing that U6atac AMO, but not control AMO or U6 AMO, resulted in inhibition of minor intron splicing (Figure 2B), whereas U6 AMO inhibited splicing of only the major introns (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 429 minor introns passed the threshold for expressed genes (FPKM > 1) in control AMO.
source: Focusing first on predicted minor introns (∼700) in the minor intron database (U12DB) (Alioto, 2007), we detected 429 that passed the threshold for expressed genes of fragments per kilobase per million mapped reads (FPKM) > 1 in control AMO.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 206 (48%) of the 429 expressed minor intron-containing genes were expressed at low levels in control and severely down-regulated (FPKM < 1) in U6atac AMO.
source: Interestingly, 206 (48%) of these were expressed at low levels in control and severely down-regulated (FPKM < 1) in U6atac AMO, suggesting that limiting amount of U6atac suppresses splicing and expression of these genes even under normal growth conditions, and that their unspliced pre-mRNAs are very unstable.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Limiting amount of U6atac suppresses splicing and expression of 206 genes even under normal growth conditions.
source: Interestingly, 206 (48%) of these were expressed at low levels in control and severely down-regulated (FPKM < 1) in U6atac AMO, suggesting that limiting amount of U6atac suppresses splicing and expression of these genes even under normal growth conditions, and that their unspliced pre-mRNAs are very unstable.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing severe down-regulation of these genes.

claim: Unspliced pre-mRNAs for 206 minor intron-containing genes are very unstable.
source: Interestingly, 206 (48%) of these were expressed at low levels in control and severely down-regulated (FPKM < 1) in U6atac AMO, suggesting that limiting amount of U6atac suppresses splicing and expression of these genes even under normal growth conditions, and that their unspliced pre-mRNAs are very unstable.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these genes are severely down-regulated when U6atac is inhibited.

claim: 44 (20%) out of 223 minor introns have little to no intronic reads in control but significant intron accumulation in U6atac AMO.
source: This showed that 44 (20%) out of these 223 have little to no intronic reads in control but significant intron accumulation in U6atac AMO (Figure 2D; CHD4, ARPC5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: For 44 minor introns, the level of U6atac snRNP is sufficient for splicing catalysis under normal growth conditions but they are extremely sensitive to U6atac decrease.
source: For these minor introns, the level of U6atac snRNP is sufficient for splicing catalysis under normal growth conditions (control AMO), but they are extremely sensitive to U6atac decrease.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing efficient splicing in control but accumulation in U6atac AMO.

claim: 81 (36%) minor introns were poorly spliced, with their unspliced pre-mRNAs clearly detectable in control and showing minimal additional response to U6atac inactivation.
source: In contrast, 81 (36%) minor introns were poorly spliced, with their unspliced pre-mRNAs clearly detectable in control and showing minimal additional response to U6atac inactivation (Figure 2E; MTBP).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For 81 minor introns, U6atac snRNP is limiting under normal growth conditions and they are predicted to splice more efficiently when U6atac level increases.
source: For these introns, U6atac snRNP is limiting under normal growth conditions and they are predicted to splice more efficiently when U6atac level increases.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing poor splicing in control conditions.

claim: Minor intron splicing dependence on U6atac abundance varied over a wide range (>20-fold).
source: Taken together, these data show a strict dependence on U6atac abundance for minor intron splicing, which actually varied over a wide range (>20-fold; Figure 2F) and thus challenges the accepted view that minor introns typically splice poorly.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The wide range of U6atac-dependent splicing could not be explained by analysis of the splice sites (AT-AC vs GT-AG) or their surrounding sequences.
source: This wide range could not be explained by analysis of the splice sites (AT-AC vs GT-AG) or their surrounding sequences (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis performed by the authors.

claim: U6atac AMO caused >twofold down-regulation in 2088 genes, including all 429 expressed minor intron genes.
source: Comparison of mRNA levels (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showed that U6atac AMO caused >twofold down-regulation in 2088 genes, including all 429 expressed minor intron genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only three genes were up-regulated by U6atac AMO.
source: Only three genes were up-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: U6atac inactivation resulted in 657 alternative splicing changes.
source: Splicing analysis revealed 657 alternative splicing changes resulting from U6atac inactivation (Figure 3A), including all 223 minor introns that showed various levels of splicing inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The major introns in minor intron-containing transcripts were spliced normally after U6atac inactivation.
source: Importantly, the major introns in these same transcripts were spliced normally.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: In a small number of minor intron-containing genes (<20), U6atac inactivation elicited alternative major intron splicing from cryptic 5′ and 3′ splice sites around the minor introns.
source: In a small number of minor intron-containing genes (<20) U6atac inactivation elicited alternative major intron splicing from cryptic 5′ and 3′ splice sites around the minor introns (e.g., C11ORF10 and ZNF207; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Alternative splicing from cryptic splice sites resulted in mRNA isoform switching without overall transcript level down-regulation.
source: This resulted in mRNA isoform switching without overall transcript level down-regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing alternative splicing patterns.

claim: Twintrons that utilize either the minor or major spliceosome by switching between adjacent U11-U12 or U1-U2 splice sites play an important role in Drosophila development.
source: Interestingly, while these effects are likely due to misplicing as a result of U6atac inhibition, they nevertheless resemble the previously described twintrons that utilize either the minor or major spliceosome by switching between adjacent U11-U12 or U1-U2 splice sites, and play an important role in Drosophila development (Scamborova et al., 2004), but has not been previously identified in human cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scamborova et al., 2004.

claim: Twintrons have not been previously identified in human cells.
source: Interestingly, while these effects are likely due to misplicing as a result of U6atac inhibition, they nevertheless resemble the previously described twintrons that utilize either the minor or major spliceosome by switching between adjacent U11-U12 or U1-U2 splice sites, and play an important role in Drosophila development (Scamborova et al., 2004), but has not been previously identified in human cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: U12 AMO had the same effects as U6atac AMO on minor intron splicing.
source: U12 AMO, tested on select minor introns (Figure 3), had the same effects as U6atac AMO, confirming that the U6atac AMO effects we observed result from the minor spliceosome inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: U6atac inactivation down-regulates or causes splicing change in all minor intron genes.
source: We conclude that U6atac decrease down-regulates or causes splicing change in all minor intron genes and that minor spliceosome inhibition reverberates widely throughout the transcriptome.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Minor spliceosome inhibition reverberates widely throughout the transcriptome.
source: We conclude that U6atac decrease down-regulates or causes splicing change in all minor intron genes and that minor spliceosome inhibition reverberates widely throughout the transcriptome.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ~2000 genes without minor introns showed expression or splicing changes.

claim: Anisomycin is a potent activator of stress-induced protein kinase p38MAPK.
source: As many of the minor intron-containing genes that were significantly affected by U6atac level change have key roles in growth regulation and cell stress signaling (Supplementary file 1B), we explored the possibility that U6atac level might change in response to specific cell stress. For this we tested the effect of anisomycin, a potent activator of stress-induced protein kinase, p38MAPK (Bunyard et al., 2003; Yong et al., 2010), and observed a ∼twofold increase in U6atac level within 4 hours (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bunyard et al., 2003; Yong et al., 2010.

claim: Anisomycin treatment resulted in approximately twofold increase in U6atac level within 4 hours.
source: For this we tested the effect of anisomycin, a potent activator of stress-induced protein kinase, p38MAPK (Bunyard et al., 2003; Yong et al., 2010), and observed a ∼twofold increase in U6atac level within 4 hours (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SB203580 is an inhibitor of p38MAPK activation.
source: Because anisomycin activates both p38MAPK and JNK, we pre-treated cells with either SB203580, an inhibitor of p38MAPK activation (Davies et al., 2000), or SP600125, an inhibitor of JNK (Heo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davies et al., 2000.

claim: SP600125 is an inhibitor of JNK.
source: Because anisomycin activates both p38MAPK and JNK, we pre-treated cells with either SB203580, an inhibitor of p38MAPK activation (Davies et al., 2000), or SP600125, an inhibitor of JNK (Heo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heo et al., 2004.

claim: SB203580 blocked the anisomycin-mediated U6atac increase.
source: While SB203580 blocked the anisomycin-mediated U6atac increase, SP600125 had only a small effect (Figure 4A), indicating that U6atac increase is predominantly due to p38MAPK activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SP600125 had only a small effect on anisomycin-mediated U6atac increase.
source: While SB203580 blocked the anisomycin-mediated U6atac increase, SP600125 had only a small effect (Figure 4A), indicating that U6atac increase is predominantly due to p38MAPK activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: U6atac increase is predominantly due to p38MAPK activation.
source: While SB203580 blocked the anisomycin-mediated U6atac increase, SP600125 had only a small effect (Figure 4A), indicating that U6atac increase is predominantly due to p38MAPK activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of p38MAPK and JNK inhibitors.

claim: ActD treatment resulted in 82% U6atac decrease.
source: In contrast to the drastic U6atac decrease after transcription inhibition with ActD (82%), co-treatment with anisomycin resulted in only about half that amount of U6atac decrease (∼40%) (Figure 4B), suggesting that cell stress-induced U6atac increase is due, at least in part, to U6atac stabilization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-treatment with ActD and anisomycin resulted in approximately 40% U6atac decrease.
source: In contrast to the drastic U6atac decrease after transcription inhibition with ActD (82%), co-treatment with anisomycin resulted in only about half that amount of U6atac decrease (∼40%) (Figure 4B), suggesting that cell stress-induced U6atac increase is due, at least in part, to U6atac stabilization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cell stress-induced U6atac increase is due, at least in part, to U6atac stabilization.
source: In contrast to the drastic U6atac decrease after transcription inhibition with ActD (82%), co-treatment with anisomycin resulted in only about half that amount of U6atac decrease (∼40%) (Figure 4B), suggesting that cell stress-induced U6atac increase is due, at least in part, to U6atac stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that anisomycin partially rescues U6atac from ActD-induced degradation.

claim: U6atac increase correlated with enhanced minor intron splicing and gene expression of a splicing reporter (LucI-minor).
source: Interestingly, the U6atac increase correlated with enhanced minor intron splicing and gene expression of a splicing reporter (LucI-minor) whose expression is strictly dependent on splicing of a minor intron, showing a twofold increase of its expression after anisomycin treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: LucI-minor reporter showed a twofold increase of its expression after anisomycin treatment.
source: Interestingly, the U6atac increase correlated with enhanced minor intron splicing and gene expression of a splicing reporter (LucI-minor) whose expression is strictly dependent on splicing of a minor intron, showing a twofold increase of its expression after anisomycin treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Intronless and major intron-containing reporters were not affected by anisomycin treatment.
source: In contrast, intronless and major intron-containing reporters (Younis et al., 2010) were not affected, indicating that the increased expression is due to enhanced minor intron splicing and not an effect on transcription or translation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Younis et al., 2010.

claim: The increased expression of LucI-minor is due to enhanced minor intron splicing and not an effect on transcription or translation.
source: In contrast, intronless and major intron-containing reporters (Younis et al., 2010) were not affected, indicating that the increased expression is due to enhanced minor intron splicing and not an effect on transcription or translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on different reporter constructs.

claim: A similar U6atac increase was observed in Jurkat T-cells and THP-1 monocytes following anisomycin treatment.
source: A similar U6atac increase was observed in Jurkat T-cells and THP-1 monocytes following anisomycin treatment (Figure 4D), indicating that U6atac increase by activated p38MAPK is a general phenomenon and not limited to HeLa cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: U6atac increase by activated p38MAPK is a general phenomenon and not limited to HeLa cells.
source: A similar U6atac increase was observed in Jurkat T-cells and THP-1 monocytes following anisomycin treatment (Figure 4D), indicating that U6atac increase by activated p38MAPK is a general phenomenon and not limited to HeLa cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar effects in multiple cell types.

claim: p38MAPK activation with anisomycin increased minor intron splicing and mRNA levels of PTEN and E2F2.
source: Similarly, p38MAPK activation with anisomycin increased minor intron splicing and mRNA levels of several endogenous genes that contain minor introns (e.g., PTEN and E2F2; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Splicing and mRNA levels of eIF3K were unaffected by anisomycin treatment.
source: Splicing and mRNA levels of eIF3K, whose minor intron splices with high efficiency in control cells, as well as GAPDH and actin, used as controls because they have no minor introns, were unaffected (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Anisomycin enhanced splicing and expression from genes whose levels are suppressed in HeLa under normal growth conditions (e.g., BRMS1L and E2F6).
source: Importantly, anisomycin also enhanced splicing and expression from genes whose levels are suppressed in HeLa under normal growth conditions (Figure 5B; e.g., BRMS1L and E2F6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PTEN's minor intron splicing increased by up to fivefold after 4 hr of anisomycin treatment.
source: To determine if the p38MAPK–induced up-regulation of minor intron splicing depends on U6atac increase, we examined, as an example, the splicing of PTEN's minor intron, which increased by up to fivefold after 4 hr of anisomycin treatment (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PTEN splicing increase was completely blocked after co-treatment with U6atac AMO.
source: This increase was completely blocked after co-treatment with U6atac AMO, even at a low amount (1 nmole) that only partially inactivates U6atac (Figure 6A), confirming that p38MAPK up-regulation of minor intron-containing mRNAs expression is strictly reliant on its ability to increase U6atac level.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: p38MAPK up-regulation of minor intron-containing mRNAs expression is strictly reliant on its ability to increase U6atac level.
source: This increase was completely blocked after co-treatment with U6atac AMO, even at a low amount (1 nmole) that only partially inactivates U6atac (Figure 6A), confirming that p38MAPK up-regulation of minor intron-containing mRNAs expression is strictly reliant on its ability to increase U6atac level.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that U6atac AMO blocks the anisomycin effect.

claim: p38MAPK activation increases transcription of TNF-α and IL-8.
source: Whereas p38MAPK activation increases transcription of several key cell physiology modulators, including up-regulation of the cytokines TNF-α and IL-8 (Figure 6B,C), which do not contain minor introns (Chang et al., 2006), production of these cytokines has been shown to be suppressed by PTEN, a minor intron-containing gene (Furumoto et al., 2006; Furgeson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C and a citation to Chang et al., 2006.

claim: TNF-α and IL-8 do not contain minor introns.
source: Whereas p38MAPK activation increases transcription of several key cell physiology modulators, including up-regulation of the cytokines TNF-α and IL-8 (Figure 6B,C), which do not contain minor introns (Chang et al., 2006), production of these cytokines has been shown to be suppressed by PTEN, a minor intron-containing gene (Furumoto et al., 2006; Furgeson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2006.

claim: Production of TNF-α and IL-8 has been shown to be suppressed by PTEN.
source: Whereas p38MAPK activation increases transcription of several key cell physiology modulators, including up-regulation of the cytokines TNF-α and IL-8 (Figure 6B,C), which do not contain minor introns (Chang et al., 2006), production of these cytokines has been shown to be suppressed by PTEN, a minor intron-containing gene (Furumoto et al., 2006; Furgeson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Furumoto et al., 2006; Furgeson et al., 2010.

claim: U6atac inactivation increased the levels of p38MAPK-mediated TNF-α and IL-8 production to more than twofold compared to control AMO.
source: As shown in Figure 6B,C, U6atac inactivation increased the levels of p38MAPK-mediated TNF-α and IL-8 production to a much higher level, >twofold compared to control AMO, suggesting that a minor intron-containing gene(s) suppresses production of these cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: A minor intron-containing gene(s) suppresses production of TNF-α and IL-8.
source: As shown in Figure 6B,C, U6atac inactivation increased the levels of p38MAPK-mediated TNF-α and IL-8 production to a much higher level, >twofold compared to control AMO, suggesting that a minor intron-containing gene(s) suppresses production of these cytokines.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that U6atac inactivation increases cytokine production.

claim: PTEN knockdown by siRNA resulted in the same effect on p38MAPK-induced TNF-α and IL-8 production as U6atac AMO.
source: To test if this is due to loss of PTEN suppression, PTEN was knocked down by siRNA (Figure 6D). This resulted in the same effect on p38MAPK-induced TNF-α and IL-8 production as U6atac AMO (Figure 6, compare panels 6E and 6F to 6B and 6C), indicating that PTEN expression, which is regulated by U6atac level, plays a role in p38MAPK-induced cytokine production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D, E, F.

claim: PTEN expression, which is regulated by U6atac level, plays a role in p38MAPK-induced cytokine production.
source: This resulted in the same effect on p38MAPK-induced TNF-α and IL-8 production as U6atac AMO (Figure 6, compare panels 6E and 6F to 6B and 6C), indicating that PTEN expression, which is regulated by U6atac level, plays a role in p38MAPK-induced cytokine production.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that PTEN knockdown phenocopies U6atac AMO effects.

claim: PTEN mRNA level was increased by 2-5 fold after anisomycin treatment.
source: We note, however, that while PTEN mRNA level was increased by 2–5 fold we have only been able to detect a small (∼20%) increase of PTEN protein level by western blot.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: PTEN protein level increased by approximately 20% after anisomycin treatment.
source: We note, however, that while PTEN mRNA level was increased by 2–5 fold we have only been able to detect a small (∼20%) increase of PTEN protein level by western blot.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Even very small changes in PTEN level are sufficient to have a strong phenotype.
source: Nevertheless, previous reports have shown that even very small changes in PTEN level are sufficient to have a strong phenotype (Alimonti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alimonti et al., 2010.

claim: Previous studies using a small number of model minor introns have led to the perception that minor introns generally splice at a slower rate than major introns.
source: Previous studies using a small number of model minor introns have led to the perception that minor introns generally splice at a slower rate than major introns and could therefore be rate limiting for the production of mRNAs that contain them (Patel et al., 2002; Singh and Padgett, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patel et al., 2002; Singh and Padgett, 2009.

claim: There has been no evidence that minor introns could be regulated.
source: However, there has been no evidence that minor introns could be regulated.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: U6atac is highly unstable relative to other snRNAs.
source: Here we discovered that U6atac is highly unstable relative to other snRNAs and its level can be rapidly up- or down-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: U6atac level can be rapidly up- or down-regulated.
source: Here we discovered that U6atac is highly unstable relative to other snRNAs and its level can be rapidly up- or down-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Modulation of U6atac amount produces a corresponding change in the amount of mRNA from many minor intron-containing genes.
source: Furthermore, modulation of U6atac amount produces a corresponding change in the amount of mRNA from many minor intron-containing genes, thus providing a novel post-transcriptional mechanism for regulating minor intron splicing and the expression of the genes that contain them, as depicted in Figure 7.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: In growing HeLa cells approximately 50% of minor intron-containing genes are suppressed by the limiting U6atac level and produce very low amounts of mRNA.
source: Interestingly, in growing HeLa cells ∼50% of minor intron-containing genes are suppressed by the limiting U6atac level and produce very low amounts of mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing 206 out of 429 genes severely down-regulated.

claim: The apparent sluggishness observed for some minor introns can be explained by the rarity of U6atac, rather than an intrinsic inefficiency of minor introns.
source: Thus, the apparent sluggishness observed for some minor introns can be explained by the rarity of U6atac, rather than an intrinsic inefficiency of minor introns.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that minor introns splice efficiently when U6atac is increased.

claim: The rapid turnover of U6atac after attenuation of either RNA polymerases II or III makes the minor spliceosome a real time sensor of transcriptional activity in cells.
source: Furthermore, the rapid turnover of U6atac after attenuation of either RNA polymerases II or III makes the minor spliceosome a real time sensor of transcriptional activity in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of U6atac's rapid response to transcriptional changes.

claim: U6atac and the many minor intron-containing genes whose expression depends on sufficient U6atac are unexpected downstream targets of p38MAPK.
source: The increased amount of U6atac following p38MAPK activation indicates that U6atac and the many minor intron-containing genes whose expression depends on sufficient U6atac are unexpected downstream targets of p38MAPK.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing p38MAPK regulation of U6atac.

claim: Minor intron-containing genes including PTEN, E2F2, E2F6 and MTBP play important roles in cell stress physiology such as regulating cytokine production.
source: These genes, including PTEN, E2F2, E2F6 and MTBP, play important roles in cell stress physiology such as regulating cytokine production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and established knowledge about these genes.

claim: PTEN is a tumor suppressor that plays key roles in cell growth and apoptosis.
source: PTEN, phosphatase and tensin homolog, is a tumor suppressor that plays key roles in cell growth and apoptosis (Tamguney and Stokoe, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tamguney and Stokoe, 2007.

claim: U6atac and the minor splicing pathway, through regulation of PTEN expression, play an antagonistic role that buffers p38MAPK-induced production of TNF-α and IL-8.
source: We show that U6atac and the minor splicing pathway, through regulation of PTEN expression, play an antagonistic role that buffers p38MAPK-induced production of TNF-α and IL-8, two major inflammatory response mediators.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: TNF-α functions in a wide range of processes including cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, lipid metabolism and coagulation.
source: TNF-α also functions in a wide range of processes including cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, lipid metabolism and coagulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TNF-α function.

claim: IL-8 is a chemo-attractant and a potent angiogenic factor.
source: IL-8 is a chemo-attractant and a potent angiogenic factor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-8 function.

claim: Activated p38MAPK phosphorylates the transcription factor ATF2, which in turn activates PTEN transcription.
source: While activated p38MAPK has been shown to phosphorylate the transcription factor ATF2, which in turn activates PTEN transcription (Shen et al., 2006; Qian et al., 2012), our data show that PTEN expression can also be regulated post-transcriptionally by the efficiency of splicing of its minor intron.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shen et al., 2006; Qian et al., 2012.

claim: PTEN expression can be regulated post-transcriptionally by the efficiency of splicing of its minor intron.
source: While activated p38MAPK has been shown to phosphorylate the transcription factor ATF2, which in turn activates PTEN transcription (Shen et al., 2006; Qian et al., 2012), our data show that PTEN expression can also be regulated post-transcriptionally by the efficiency of splicing of its minor intron.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Minor introns and snRNPs have been lost at multiple points during eukaryotic evolution.
source: Indeed, despite their early evolutionary origin, minor introns and snRNPs have been lost at multiple points during eukaryotic evolution (Bartschat and Samuelsson, 2010), suggesting that, in contrast to the major spliceosome, they are not absolutely essential.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bartschat and Samuelsson, 2010.

claim: Minor introns and snRNPs are not absolutely essential, in contrast to the major spliceosome.
source: Indeed, despite their early evolutionary origin, minor introns and snRNPs have been lost at multiple points during eukaryotic evolution (Bartschat and Samuelsson, 2010), suggesting that, in contrast to the major spliceosome, they are not absolutely essential.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that they have been lost in some lineages.

claim: Minor intron-containing genes that typically contain a single minor intron amidst many major ones function in diverse cellular processes that are critical for cell growth and organism development.
source: Minor intron-containing genes that typically contain a single minor intron amidst many major ones function in diverse cellular processes that are critical for cell growth and organism development (Otake et al., 2002; Alioto, 2007; Abdel-Salam et al., 2011; Edery et al., 2011; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Otake et al., 2002; Alioto, 2007; Abdel-Salam et al., 2011; Edery et al., 2011; He et al., 2011.

claim: A single minor intron is sufficient to regulate the expression of an entire pre-mRNA.
source: Indeed, as our RNA-seq show, a single minor intron is sufficient to regulate the expression of an entire pre-mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing effects on full-length transcripts.

claim: The conservation of minor introns over more than 500 million years demonstrates the effectiveness of this gene regulation mechanism.
source: The conservation of this design principle over >500 million years (Burge et al., 1998; Shukla and Padgett, 1999; Russell et al., 2006) demonstrates the effectiveness of this gene regulation mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burge et al., 1998; Shukla and Padgett, 1999; Russell et al., 2006.

claim: More than 120 million RNA-seq reads were obtained for each sample.
source: More than 120 million RNA-seq reads were obtained for each sample, with ∼70% of these mapping to 9799 and 8397 genes in control and U6atac AMO-treated cells, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Table 1.

claim: Approximately 70% of RNA-seq reads mapped to 9799 genes in control cells and 8397 genes in U6atac AMO-treated cells.
source: More than 120 million RNA-seq reads were obtained for each sample, with ∼70% of these mapping to 9799 and 8397 genes in control and U6atac AMO-treated cells, respectively (Table 1).
